steps: Uncrate & remove the brick pack
Remove the crating top, supports and plastic cover, then take the brick pack out of the firebox. Fit the firebricks only once the stove is in its final location and the chimney is installed.

Remove the wood crating top and supports and the plastic cover, then take the brick pack out of the firebox. Install the firebricks after the stove is in its final location and the chimney is installed.

  • The appliance must be installed with the pedestal or leg kit attached (rating label).
  • Never install it in a makeshift or temporary manner, in any fireplace, or connected to an air distribution duct.
  • Contact local building or fire officials about restrictions, permits and installation inspection.
Floor protection

On a combustible floor, lay continuous non-combustible ember protection: USA 16" to the front and 8" to the sides of the fuel loading door opening (min. 33" × 34 3/8"); Canada 18" on the firing side and 8" on the other sides (min. 43 3/4" × 45 1/8").

On a combustible floor, use continuous non-combustible ember protection.

USA · front16" from the fuel loading door opening
USA · sides8" to the sides of the fuel loading door opening
USA · minimum33" wide × 34 3/8" deep
Canada · firing side18"
Canada · other sides8"
Canada · minimum43 3/4" wide × 45 1/8" deep

The USA text also requires protection under the chimney connector and 2" beyond each side with any horizontal venting.

Confirm the US side extension: p. 14 gives 8" to the sides of the fuel loading door opening; the rating label (p. 3) lists US values G 16", H 5", I 0" on a lettered drawing whose reference points the text doesn't define.
Position to clearances
Place the stove and floor protector to the clearance chart: 10" side wall, 10" back wall and 7" corner with a single-wall connector; 8", 8" and 5" with a listed double-wall connector.

Single-wall · side / back / corner10" / 10" / 7"
Double-wall · side / back / corner8" / 8" / 5"
Alcove7' min. height · 3' max. depth
Combustibles in front of the unit48" (venting drawings, pp. 18-19)

Connector-to-wall distances are on the clearance cards (see the confirm notes there). Don't obstruct the space beneath the heater. Clearances may be reduced with heat shielding per CSA B365 or NFPA 211 with local approval; for close clearances, use a listed double-wall connector.
Check the chimney

Use a ULC-S629 or UL-103HT listed stainless chimney, or a lined masonry chimney suitable for solid fuel, with a 6" flue serving only this stove, at least 15 feet of system height and an exit 3 feet above the roof.
Mark & install the chimney

Hang a plumb-bob over the exact center of the flue pipe to mark the ceiling and roof; check joists and rafters, reconfirm clearances, then install the listed chimney through to the rain cap per its maker's directions.
Fit the chimney connector

Slip the crimped edge of the pipe inside the stove collar and fix it with three screws through the collar holes; stack the remaining lengths to the finished chimney height and join them with the maker's approved adapter.

Slip the crimped edge of the smoke pipe inside the stove collar and secure it with three screws through the holes provided. Install the remaining lengths one on top of the other up to the finished height of the chimney, using the manufacturer's approved adapter; a slip section makes this easier.

Single-wall (smoke pipe) connector

  • 6" diameter, 24 gauge black pipe, clean and in new condition, as short and straight as possible.
  • Crimped (male) ends pointing down; secure every joint and the collar with 3 sheet metal screws.
  • Never through an attic, roof space, closet or similar concealed space, floor, or ceiling.
  • With a listed chimney, consult local or national codes for the connector installation.

Double-wall connector

Use a listed double-wall connector and install it to the chimney/connector manufacturer's requirements.

Offsets: screw all sections of listed connector, offset elbows and chimney together with at least three sheet metal screws per joint, and support the chimney with its maker's listed offset support. Figure 9 (p. 18) shows an alternate up-and-out install with a 12" minimum first section of pipe; the unit may be harder to start, so give the first section as much vertical length as possible.
Combustion air

Room air enters through the opening in the ash box enclosure. For outside air (required in mobile homes), run 4" metal duct through the floor or the wall behind, fit the 4" adapter to the ash box enclosure, and secure the stove to the structure.
Wall pass-through (if used)
Where the connector must pass through a combustible wall, build it to CAN/CSA-B365 or one of the NFPA 211 systems A-D, and maintain the vapour barrier where components reach the exterior.

Where passage through a combustible wall or partition is wanted, the installation must conform to CAN/CSA-B365 (p. 16). The manual details four NFPA 211 systems:

System A · 12 in. to combustiblesMin. 3.5 in. brick wall with 12 in. of brick from the clay liner to combustibles; fireclay liner min. 5/8 in. wall thickness
System B · 9 in. to combustiblesSolid-insulated listed chimney length, 1 in. or more insulation, min. 9 in. air space
System C · 6 in. to combustibles24 gauge connector with ventilated 24 gauge thimble, two 1 in. air channels, min. 6 in. glass fiber insulation
System D · 2 in. to combustiblesSolid-insulated listed chimney length 2 in. larger inside diameter, 1 in. or more insulation, min. 2 in. air space; min. length 12 in.

Maintain the vapour barrier wherever the chimney or other components penetrate to the exterior.

Confirm wall pass-throughs: the rating label (p. 3) says do not pass a chimney connector through a combustible wall or ceiling; pp. 16 and 20-21 describe wall pass-throughs to CAN/CSA-B365 and NFPA 211.
Mobile home requirements
Use only a listed double-wall connector with a ULC-S629 or UL-103HT listed chimney, an outside air supply and legs anchored to the floor; never in a sleeping room, and no horizontal connector.

• Listed double-wall connector only, with a compatible ULC-S629 or UL-103HT listed chimney system; clearances as for the double-wall connector (Figure 15).
  • Outside air supply must be used (outside air kit).
  • Anchor the stove permanently to the floor through the holes in the bottoms of the legs.
  • Do not install in a sleeping room. Horizontal connector not permitted. Don't connect to a flue serving another appliance.
  • Maintain the structural integrity of the floor, walls and ceiling/roof.

These are in addition to the residential requirements. Consult local building codes and fire authorities for approval.
Install the firebricks
Start with the rear wall, then each side wall, then the floor; a gap stays behind the ash dump and one brick is left over as a spare.

A8 7/8" x 4 3/8" x 1 1/4"
B8 7/8" x 2 1/8" x 1 1/4"
C5 3/4" x 4 3/8" x 1 1/4"
D4 3/8" x 3 1/4" x 1 1/4"
E7" x 3 1/4" x 1 1/4"
F4 1/4" x 2 1/8" x 1 1/4"
  1. Rear wall: stand an "A" brick behind the brick-rail tab and slide it toward the center; slide the next "A" under the tab; repeat for the other rear "A" bricks.
  2. Side walls: two "A" bricks and a narrow "B" against each wall, a "D" on top tucked behind the brick rail, then an "E" slid under the side brick-rail tab.
  3. Floor: two "A" bricks, a third "A" against the rear wall, "C" beside the ash dump against the left wall, then the front row "F", "B", "F".

Positions are shown in Figures 16-24.

light.title: Lighting a fire
light.html:
Build every fire right on the firebricks. Don't use a grate or andirons.

  1. Move the air control to High, all the way to the left, and open the door.
  2. Put crumpled newspaper in the center of the stove and crisscross several pieces of dry kindling over it. Add a few small pieces of dry wood on top.
  3. Light the paper. Leave the door open about 1/2" to 1" until the kindling is fully in flames. Don't leave the stove while the door is open.
  4. Add a few small logs and close the door.
  5. Once there's a good bed of coals and the wood has charred, start normal burning.
Never use gasoline, lantern fuel, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or any similar liquid to start or freshen up a fire.

Your first 2-3 fires

The paint bakes on during the first 2-3 fires and gives off smoke and fumes. Open all windows and doors. Bring the stove slowly to a medium burn for about 45 minutes, then to a high burn for another 45-60 minutes. Follow the Stove Bright paint sheet that came with your stove. Smoke detectors may go off more often while the paint cures. Don't disconnect them.

air.title: Using the air control
air.html:
The air control sets how hard the fire burns. High ("H") is all the way to the left; "L" is low.

  • Use High only to start a fire or to preheat a fresh load. It is the maximum firing rate.
  • After each load, leave the air fairly wide open for the first 10 to 30 minutes, while most of the smoke is made. After 30 minutes or so you can turn it down a lot without much smoke.
  • Smoke pouring down the glass (a "waterfall") means you turned it down too soon or too low.

The right setting depends on your wood, the weather, your house and your chimney. Find yours by trial and error and note it for next time.

If you have the optional blower

With the air control on L, run the blower on Low. Between L and H, use any speed. Set the rocker switch on the fan housing to Auto and it starts as the stove heats up and stops after it cools, or to Man to run it yourself.

Don't alter the air control. The minimum burn rate is set at the factory; changing it is against federal regulations, and tampering voids the warranty.

reload.title: Reloading & overnight burns
reload.html:
Adding wood

  1. Set the air control to High and give the fire time to brighten.
  2. Open the door slowly. That keeps smoke from puffing back into the room.
  3. Load logs right to left, up to 18" long, placed so air can flow between them. Always use dry wood.
  4. Don't pile wood so high, or so that it's hazardous when you open the door. Make sure no logs stick out to hit the glass.

Small loads burn cleanest: two or three logs at a time, or 1/4 to 1/2 of a full load.

Overnight burns

Use unsplit logs. Char the wood completely on the maximum setting before you turn the air down for the night. Never try an overnight burn with green or wet wood.

Restarting from embers

  1. Open the door and rake the hot embers toward the front.
  2. Add a couple of dry, split logs on top and close the door.
  3. Set the air control to High. The logs should catch within a few minutes.
  4. Once the wood has charred, set the air back where you want it.

wood.title: Choosing & testing your wood
wood.html:
Burn natural wood only. Air-dried, seasoned hardwood gives the most heat and the least smoke. Season wood for six months or more and store it under cover, away from flames and heat.

Never burn

  • Wet, green or unseasoned wood, or salt-water wood
  • Treated wood, railroad ties, plywood, particleboard, construction or demolition debris
  • Garbage, cardboard and paper products, lawn clippings or yard waste
  • Coal or charcoal, solvents, paints, petroleum or asphalt products, manure or animal remains, or anything with rubber, plastic or asbestos

Paper, cardboard, sawdust or wax fire starters are fine for lighting. Never barbecue in the stove.

Test a piece

Put a large piece on a good bed of coals. Dry wood burns on more than one side within one minute. Damp wood turns black and lights within three minutes. If it sizzles, hisses and blackens without lighting in five minutes, it's soaked. Don't burn it.

Wet wood can cut heat output by up to 25% and builds creosote fast.

ash.title: Emptying the ashes
ash.html:
Take out ashes only when the stove is cold: the fire has burned down and cooled, and the ash is 3" to 4" deep. Leave about 1" of ash on the firebox floor. It helps keep a hot charcoal bed.

Using the ash dump

  1. The handle is under the ash lip on the left side. Pull it out 1/2" and turn it clockwise to unlock the ash dump.
  2. Hold the handle open and pull ashes into the opening. Leave large embers; they still have heat in them.
  3. Release the handle and push it in to lock. Check that the ash dump door is properly engaged, then fill the cavity with the remaining ash, level with the floor.
  4. Lift out the ash pan, empty it into a metal container, and seat the pan back properly.
Never burn with the ash dump door open. Keep it closed whenever there's a fire.

Storing ashes

Use a metal container with a tight-fitting lid. Set it on a non-combustible floor or on the ground, well away from anything that burns. Keep ashes in the closed container until every cinder is completely cool, and don't put other waste in it.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
Clean the glass with fireplace glass cleaner, and only when the stove is cold. Never scrape it with anything that could scratch it, and don't use abrasive cleaners.

What the deposit tells you

  • Light brown dust that wipes off easily: good combustion and dry, seasoned wood. Your pipes and chimney are probably fairly clean.
  • Black, greasy deposit that's hard to remove: wet or green wood and too slow a burn. The same buildup is forming at least as fast in your chimney.

Glass that keeps getting dirty can also mean a leaking door gasket, or a door latch that needs checking.

Protect the glass

  • Don't slam the door, and make sure no logs stick out to hit the glass.
  • If the glass cracks or breaks, replace it before you use the stove again. Use only 10-1/2" x 16-1/2" x 5 mm ceramic glass from your dealer.

chimney.title: Creosote & chimney fires
chimney.html:
Slow, smoky fires leave creosote, a tar that builds up in the chimney and can catch fire. Have the chimney connector and chimney inspected at least once every two months during the heating season, and have creosote removed once it's 3 mm or more.

While you're learning the stove, check for creosote daily until you know how often you need to clean. Hotter fires leave less: you may need weekly cleaning in mild weather, while monthly is usually enough in the coldest months. Use a certified professional (NFI or CSIA in the U.S.).

Signs of a chimney fire

  • Flames and sparks shooting out of the top of the chimney
  • A roaring sound
  • The chimney vibrating

If it happens

  1. Get everyone ready to leave, with a meeting place outside.
  2. Close the air control on the stove.
  3. Call the fire department. Keep a fire extinguisher handy.
  4. Before the next fire, have the chimney cleaned and checked for stress and cracks, and check the combustibles around the chimney and the roof.

safety.title: Safety around the stove
safety.html:
• The stove is hot whenever it's running. Keep children, clothing and furniture away; touching it can burn skin.
  • Hot glass burns. Don't touch it until it has cooled, and never let children touch it.
  • Keep the loading door closed while the fire burns. Open it only to add wood. The stove isn't designed for open-door burning.
  • Keep gasoline, kerosene, lighter fluid and similar liquids well away from the stove, and never use them to start a fire.
  • Don't store wood, furniture or newspapers within the stove's clearances or the space you need for loading and ash removal.
  • Smoke and carbon monoxide detectors are strongly recommended in the area where the stove is installed.

Signs it's burning too hot

A glowing red top or vent pipe means the stove is over-firing. An uncontrollable burn, or a glowing red stove part or chimney, means too much draft. Don't leave either uncorrected: over-firing can permanently damage the stove and chimney, can be hazardous, and may void the warranty. Use the High setting only to start a fire or preheat a fresh load.

care.title: Routine checks
care.html:
Look for cracks, heavy corrosion, burned-out sections or bad warping:

WeeklyFirebrick (cracks); door gasket (sagging, placement, damage)
MonthlyBrick rails and their tabs, air riser tube at the back, back of the airwash chamber, baffle locking pin, boost openings
BlowerVacuum the grill openings at least every six months
  • Door gasket: the 7/8" fiberglass rope needs only light pressure to seal. Replace it when needed with the kit from your Pacific Energy dealer.
  • Baffle: some warping, up to 1/4", is normal. Replace it if it warps more, cracks or breaks.
  • Firebricks: replace broken or missing bricks.
  • Boost air: keep the front of the firebox clear of heavy ash.
Call your dealer about any damage. Running the stove with broken parts can damage other parts and may void the warranty. Use only manufacturer-supplied materials for repairs.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
Pacific Energy covers the original registered purchaser:

Limited lifetime (10 years), parts onlyPorcelain finish, glass (thermal breakage, not impact), plating, firebox, baffle
3 years, parts and laborAny defective part, including blowers, speed controls and thermal switches

Not covered

  • Firebrick, gaskets and ceramic fiber blankets
  • Firebox rails and heat shields (not in the lifetime coverage), and labor under the lifetime coverage
  • Misuse, abuse, improper installation, accident, lack of maintenance, or modification

Excessive draft, heating too large an area, or contaminated fuel (high sodium, plastics, chemicals) can void it, as can tampering with the air control or over-firing.

For a claim, go to your Pacific Energy dealer with proof of purchase, the purchase date, and the model name and serial number. The serial number is on the certification label or on the cover of the manual.

This is a summary. The full terms are in the official manual.

specOutput.title: Output, efficiency & emissions
specOutput.html:
EPA BTU output13,494 to 23,186 btu/hr
HHV tested efficiency72%
LHV tested efficiency78%
EPA certified emissions1.9 g/hr
FuelSeasoned cord wood

Weighted averages tested to CSA B415; the output range comes from the low and high EPA tests using Douglas Fir dimensional lumber. Meets the EPA 2020 crib wood particulate emission standards (Method 28R). Listed to CAN/ULC S627 and UL 1482 as a solid-fuel room heater, also for mobile homes.

The manual covers the Alderlea T4 LE and the T4 LE Classic with this one set of figures.

specWood.title: Wood length & loading
specWood.html:
Ideal wood length16 inches
Maximum wood length18 inches

Load right to left with air space between logs; unsplit logs for overnight burns. Burn directly on the firebricks, with no grate or andirons. Don't load to a height that would be hazardous when opening the door.

specFlue.title: Flue & chimney
specFlue.html:
Flue size6 inches, same as the stove outlet
Minimum system height15 feet, measured from the base of the appliance
Chimney exit3 feet above the roof and two feet above the highest projection within 10 feet

Chimney: ULC-S629 or UL-103HT listed stainless, or a masonry chimney suitable for solid fuel that is lined, in good condition and meets codes. Reducing or increasing the flue size may hurt performance. Don't connect to a flue serving another appliance.

The manual says both chimney system and connector must be listed: in the USA, UL-103 HT listed connector and chimney; in Canada, ULC S-641 listed double-wall connector and ULC-S629 listed chimney. It also gives single-wall smoke-pipe rules for residential installs.

specAir.title: Combustion air
specAir.html:
Outside air · floor4" metal venting behind the ash box enclosure, 4" OAIR adapter, 4" i.d. flexible metal ducting
Outside air · wall4" wall air intake kit, 4" intake adapter on the rear of the ash box enclosure
Room airThrough the opening in the ash box enclosure
Mobile homeOutside air required

Check local code or CAN/CSA-B365 first. A floor inlet must draw from a ventilated crawl space or be ducted outdoors; a well-ventilated crawl space needn't be extended outside. The inlet gets a rodent screen (hooded, or a 90° elbow turned down). Outside air in a residential install requires securing the unit to the structure so the duct can't be dislodged.

Keep the living space well ventilated: negative pressure can pull fumes into the room, and in extreme cold at very slow burns the exposed chimney may ice up.

specBlower.title: Optional blower
specBlower.html:
Kit#11140001
Electrical rating (p. 24)115 volts A.C. · 1.1 amps
Fan electrical rating (label, p. 3)115V, 60HZ, 1.0 AMP
Fan output140 CFM

Three-prong power cord; can be installed at any time per the kit's instructions. Route the cord away from the heater, never beneath it. Rocker switch: Auto (comes on as the stove heats up, shuts off once it has cooled) or Man (bypasses the sensing device). Vacuum the grill openings at least every six months.

Confirm the blower current: the manual gives 1.1 amps on p. 24 and 1.0 amp on the rating label (p. 3).

review.notes: One manual (100003978, 061026-32) covers both catalog models: p. 3 says it describes the 'ALDERLEA T4 LE and ALDERLEA T4 LE Classic'. Every figure is captioned 'T4 LE' and no number differs between the two, so there are no per-model rows. The rating label (p. 3) lists Vista LE, Vista Classic LE and Alderlea T4 LE (no separate T4 Classic line); the Vista LE values were left out. The parts list (p. 27) offers castings in metallic black paint, Majolica brown enamel and ivory enamel (the catalog's Sunset Red isn't listed); the paint-curing section (p. 5) doesn't distinguish enamel finishes. Page 3 is scrambled in doc1.txt; HHV 72% / LHV 78% and the per-model D/E/F label values were confirmed from the raw extract's reading order. Not transcribed (drawings only): Figure 5 dimensions (p. 13) and the venting drawings' unlabelled values; the label's floor-protector letters and Figure 8's connector dimensions are quoted only in confirm notes. The 48" to combustibles in front of the unit and the 12" minimum first pipe section come from text labels on the venting drawings (pp. 18-19). French-only label text (p. 3) lists required parts for mobile home 'or alcove' installs (outside air kit plus listed connector/chimney); the English line names mobile homes only.
